content: The Adapted Health Visitor Intervention Program implemented in Cape Town, South Africa, demonstrated that over 90% of participants felt supported, trusted the providers, and were able to openly communicate with them. This led to improved abilities in responding to their infants and solving problems. However, a feasibility evaluation of the Thinking Healthy Program (Atif et al., 2017) identified several barriers to implementing peer-delivered programs. These included concerns about confidentiality among peers, stigma associated with mental health issues such as sadness and depression being labeled as madness, lack of financial support, and cultural traditions that restricted mothers from attending group meetings without male accompaniment. Regarding the balance of effects, there is uncertainty about whether the desirable effects of psychosocial interventions outweigh the undesirable ones. None of the studies included in the systematic review reported any adverse effects of the reviewed psychosocial interventions. The resource requirements for psychosocial interventions during the intrapartum period are uncertain, primarily due to a lack of cost-effectiveness analyses in most of the included studies. However, pharmacological interventions are generally expected to have lower resource requirements compared to non-pharmacological interventions. Psychosocial interventions for perinatal mental health issues could potentially reduce the prevalence of common mental disorders (CMDs) and associated costs, such as medication use, while requiring more visits from healthcare workers. Broader effects, such as impacts on the baby, other children, and the partner, also need to be considered. The Healthy Activity Program (HAP) showed superior results in secondary outcomes, including reduced disability, fewer days out of work, and decreased intimate partner violence against women. The incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained was $9,333 (95% CI: $3,862–$28,169), with an 87% probability of being cost-effective from a health system perspective. The cost-effectiveness of the HAP program was sustained at 12-month follow-ups, and it was found to be more cost-effective than usual care, with an incremental cost per QALY gained of −$1,721 and a 95% likelihood of cost-effectiveness. In the recent Lancet series on early childhood development, the cost of integrating the Thinking Healthy component of the mhGAP into existing maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) services was estimated at $2 per person per year, indicating that maternal mental health interventions can be added to MNCH services at minimal additional cost (Richter et al., 2017). The cost-effectiveness of psychosocial interventions has also been supported by a systematic review summarizing 13 studies on economic evaluations of such interventions in high-income countries (Morrell et al., 2016). The certainty of evidence regarding resource requirements is low, as no included studies provided sufficient data. The cost-effectiveness of interventions likely varies, with limited evidence available from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Most evidence is restricted to high-income settings. The impact on health equity is likely to increase because perinatal depression is a significant public health concern, particularly among mothers in LMICs. It leads to poor emotional, physical, and behavioral outcomes for mothers and adverse outcomes for children, such as low birth weight, stunting, preterm birth, respiratory disorders, and poor academic performance. Establishing cost-effective and culturally sensitive intervention programs in LMICs is crucial, given the lack of specialist and non-specialist mental health workforce (WHO, 2014). The acceptability of these interventions is likely high among affected populations in LMICs. High retention rates were observed in many studies, and attitudes of mothers and communities were generally positive. Healthcare professionals also reported positive attitudes toward psychosocial interventions, with strong support from local communities. Peer-delivered programs, such as the Thinking Healthy Program, inspired social support, satisfaction, and opportunities for skill development, although lack of financial support was a barrier (Atif et al., 2016). The feasibility of implementing these interventions is likely high. The meta-analysis indicated good effectiveness across several outcomes, although the quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate. Intervention features, such as the number of sessions and duration, could potentially be adapted to specific settings, but more evidence is needed to confirm this. Costs can be reduced by employing trained and supported non-specialists and peers, although these interventions may have lower effect sizes compared to specialist-delivered interventions. Integrated interventions utilizing pre-established healthcare systems could further reduce associated costs.
